It is one move (slow drift and resolve) for its whole length; there is no second idea or surprise of the kind the Vertigo spirals provide
The credits sit centred in a plain sans that does not engage with the hero letterforms; integrating them as A and B do would lift every frame

The composition logic is the same in every frame (a crop of a letter around a centred credit), so the surprise rests on the final reveal alone
tells: The logotype itself is the whole set. Extreme crops of glowing outlined serif letters slide past the credits and slowly come together into the full title, so the frames show choreography and a payoff.
The red neon glow has real softness, bloom and grain, and it reads as backlit film or a lit-up book cover rather than a flat vector stroke.
The choice of an ITC Benguiat-style face and the lockup with ruled lines are a precise period reference that does narrative work.
Against it: the credits are centred, small, in a plain sans, and sit in the same position in every frame. The repetition is deliberate, but the composition of the credits barely changes.

Clear choreography: the camera pulls back from abstract glowing strokes to legible fragments ('RANG', 'ING') and finally to the full lockup. The reveal builds over the six frames

Restraint is the idea: nothing but type and light, which serves the 80s Stephen King / paperback-cover reference

Each frame builds a credit around a monogram initial (&, TMP, J, FX) that breaks apart into simulated smoke or powder. That is a real typographic system tied to each speaker, not a slide with the words swapped.

The fluid and particle simulation has volume, internal shading and falloff that change from frame to frame. The fourth and fifth frames show the letters dissolving into a pigment cloud, so the motion has weight and a direction.
It ends on a proper title card (SEMI-PERMANENT / SYDNEY | 2014) with a deliberate cut-out treatment in the letters, so the sequence lands somewhere.

Against it: the single teal accent on a dark ground with a perspective grid and bokeh is very much the 2014 Cinema 4D conference-opener look. The grotesk sans with tracked-caps subtitles under the names is close to the default.
gaps: Replace the stock vignette, grid floor and bokeh with an environment or material that says something about this conference. Right now the backdrop could belong to any event.
Take the palette beyond one teal with a dark falloff. Bring in a second colour or a material shift so the frames are not tonally identical.

Push the type past a clean grotesk with small tracked captions. Make the scale contrast more extreme, or let the smoke actually build the letterforms, so the typography is the idea rather than a carrier for the effect.

tells: The central idea belongs to this film alone: an extreme close-up of an eye, washed blood red, gives birth to Lissajous and spirograph spirals. The obsession, the disorientation and the act of looking all become one image.
The palette is strange and deliberate. Saturated red photography gives way to black fields with magenta and then mint-green line figures, and colour is used for narrative effect.

The structure is a loop: eye, spiral, abstract spirals, then back to the eye for the director's credit. The spirals change shape and colour between frames, which implies continuous rotation and growth.
The slab-serif outline title has a period voice. The credit blocks are set against the spirals with real scale contrast and asymmetric placement, as in the art-direction frame.
gaps: This is the reference point here, so the gaps are small. Some middle credit cards fall back on a conventional stacked list beside the figure.
The abstract spiral frames sit on flat black. Some photographic texture carried through from the eye would tighten the link between the two halves.
Some credit text is very small against the spirals. Holding the reading hierarchy a little better would help.

tells: The idea is witty and specific to the film: every credit is set as packaging for its own invented cigarette brand. The satire of tobacco marketing is built into the form.

The typography has a strong point of view and changes from card to card. There is a ribbon banner, script, a serif with LIGHTS, a geometric sans with a sunburst, an Art Deco face for the menthol pack and a script-over-bold lockup, each matched to a believable pack style.

There is real print texture: worn paper, foil-gold borders, registration marks, halftone engravings of a dog, an eagle and a plane. The palette moves between blue, cream, orange, red and green without losing coherence.
Every frame works as a poster on its own, and the last frame of rows of filters works as a punchline.
gaps: The frames suggest mostly cuts or pans across flat packs. Each card plays the same move, so the choreography between cards is weaker than the transformations in B.
Each pack is close-cropped and front-on. Varying the camera, depth or material, such as cellophane glint or the fold of a pack, would add physical space.
The concept is one strong joke repeated six times. A structural escalation or a turn, the way B returns to the eye, would lift it to the top tier.

tells: Conference/event title sequence (Semi-Permanent Sydney 2014): each speaker gets their initials or a glyph (&, TMP, J, FX) that breaks into simulated teal smoke or powder, which is a real system rather than a one-off effect
Fluid/particle sims are art-directed: the smoke fills the letter counters, and frame 5 dissolves the type entirely into a powder burst before the final logo resolves, so the sequence clearly builds
Scale contrast between the giant monogram and the small tracked-caps name and role is deliberate and shows a hierarchy system

Against it: dark vignetted ground, a perspective grid, a single cyan/teal accent and a generic geometric grotesk. That is the 2014 'epic conference opener' look and sits uncomfortably close to the template tells
Every frame uses the same layout of centred glyph, name and small caps on dark, so variety comes only from the sim and not from composition
gaps: Find a concept tied to the event or the speakers instead of 'letters explode into coloured smoke'. Vertigo's spiral says something about the film; this smoke says nothing about Semi-Permanent
Break the one-accent-on-dark palette and the generic grotesk: commission or choose a face with a point of view and let colour change per speaker or per act
Vary composition and camera between cards (crops, scale, letterforms bleeding off frame the way Stranger Things does) so the frames stop reading as one layout with the names swapped

tells: Saul Bass's Vertigo (1958). The idea is inseparable from the film: an extreme close-up of an eye, from which Lissajous/spirograph spirals emerge, makes obsession and dizziness visible
Red-monochrome photography alternates with black fields of violet and then green line-work. The palette is unusual and narrative, and the green anticipates the film's Judy/Madeleine green
Slab-serif outline title type sits directly in the eye and is integrated with the image; on the black frames the credits are set as justified blocks around the spiral form
The frame sequence shows a structure: the eye, the spiral born in the pupil, a series of mutating spirals, then a return to the eye for the director credit. It is choreographed and bookended
Every frame works as a poster; the line-work has real optical depth and moiré
gaps: Serves as the benchmark
The credit blocks on the spiral frames are somewhat dense and conventional next to the title card
The mid-section spirals read as variations rather than escalation; a modern jury might ask for one more surprise in the middle act

tells: Thank You For Smoking: every credit is rendered as a different period cigarette pack (Blended Mild crest, Honey-Toasted Lights hound, Lights eagle and stars, a red filter pack with sunburst, a Menthol pack with palm and plane, and a final row of filters)

The typography is the idea. Each name gets a pastiche face that fits its brand (script, Clarendon-like serif, condensed sans, Art Deco menthol caps), with perfect period detailing: 'UNDERAGE SALE PROHIBITED', 'PREMIUM BLEND', tax stamps
Paper texture, print registration, foil gold and halftone illustration give it real material quality
The palette changes card to card while staying in a coherent mid-century packaging world; the irony is pointed and memorable
Tight crops show the camera moving across and over the packs rather than presenting them flat
gaps: Motion is mostly slow pans across flat print; it needs more choreography between cards (transitions, turning or folding packs) to match Vertigo's sense of progression
Light is graphic and flat by design; some physical depth (the foil catching light, the cellophane) would lift it from a clever print idea to a cinematic one
The concept is a single repeated gag; there is no structural turn or escalation before the director card

tells: A specific idea that fits only this film: every credit is set as a fake cigarette-pack label, so the title sequence is itself an ad for the product the film satirises

Typography changes with every pack and suits each brand: a banner serif with a crest, a brush script ('Cameron Bright'), a condensed slab for 'LIGHTS', wide caps over a sunburst, a deco serif for menthol, and an italic script paired with heavy caps for the director

Period-correct printed texture: gold foil stripes, slight off-register and paper grain, engraved animals and crests, scalloped borders, and small copy like 'honey-toasted tobacco lights' and 'underage sale prohibited'
Each frame has its own palette (royal blue/gold, orange/cream, red-white-blue, red/navy, mint/green, red/white with filter tips), yet the whole set reads as one system
The final frame, a row of cigarette filters under the director credit, is a witty payoff
gaps: From the stills, the motion looks like mostly lateral pans across flat packs; choreography between frames needs to escalate as it does in B, rather than stay a catalogue of tracking shots
Every frame is a crop of a single surface; the piece needs one shift in scale or depth (opening a pack, a dimensional reveal) to break the flatness
The structure is a gallery of variations, so it lacks the build to a single emotional climax that B's return to the eye achieves

tells: The concept carries the film's theme: an extreme close-up of an eye gives way to Lissajous/spirograph spirals that stand for obsession and vertigo, then the sequence returns to the eye
A bold palette: a monochrome red-tinted face, black voids, then violet and later acid-green line forms. Nothing about it is a default
An expressive outlined slab/Clarendon title, against tightly ranked right-aligned credit blocks with a clear hierarchy (small role labels, larger names)
The frames show real choreography: a photographic face, the spiral emerging from the pupil, abstract spirals that turn and change colour, then the eye again. This is a closed loop with tension in it
Photographic skin, lashes and specular highlights next to precise generated line work: two materials playing against each other on purpose
gaps: The credit-block layouts on black are functional and a little static compared with the hero frames
The middle section leans on repeating the spiral motif, so variety drops slightly between frames 3 and 5
The title type sits on top of the image rather than being built into it, unlike A, where the type is the object

tells: A dark vignetted ground, a faint 3D grid floor, and a single teal accent throughout: very close to the generic 'tasteful' look
The type is a stock geometric/grotesk sans, with small tracked caps under bold names, laid out like a slide

The default grotesk with tracked-caps subtitles should be replaced by type with a point of view and real scale contrast that interacts with the image
